title: the community
hookLine: the community; why the Buddha said it's the whole of the path
tomorrow: the Buddha's past lives as animals

cards: New habits are hard to keep alone. The gym, eating better, an earlier bedtime, meditating every day. A week goes great, and then, quietly, it doesn't.
The habits that last often have someone else in them. A running partner. A class.
A friend who texts, you coming? Plenty of things are easier with company. The Buddha seems to have thought so too.
When his attendant Ananda suggested friends were half the path, the Buddha corrected him.

teach.b: Sangha. The word means an assembly, a gathering, a community.
It's the third of the three jewels you bowed to on day two. The Buddha, the teacher. The Dharma, the teaching.
And the Sangha, the community that practices it. In its narrowest sense, the sangha means the monks and nuns.
The Buddha is remembered describing a fourfold assembly: monks, nuns, laymen and laywomen.
Today some Buddhists, especially in Western groups, use sangha for any group that practices together: a temple congregation, a Tuesday-night sitting group, the people you meditate with online.
Here's the story from the discourses.
Ananda, the Buddha's attendant, and his cousin by tradition, says to him one day: it seems to me that good friendship is half of the holy life. And the Buddha answers: don't say that, Ananda.
Good friendship, good companionship, is the whole of the holy life. Not half. The whole thing.
He explains that a person with good friends can be expected to develop the whole path. The friend doesn't replace the practice. The friend is how the practice keeps going.

When an old English translator met the word sangha, he reached for a very English word: the Church. It's a clumsy fit in some ways, but it catches something true. A sangha isn't a club you join because you already agree.
It's the people who keep walking beside you on the days you'd rather quit.

how: Buddhists take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma and the Sangha, often by reciting the three refuges in Pali; they support monastic communities with food and gifts, and gather with lay sanghas to meditate, chant, study and celebrate festivals.

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.
p: the Buddha, the Dharma, the Sangha
said friendship is half the path
an old translator's word for sangha

s: sangha can only mean monks and nuns
narrowly it does; the Buddha also spoke of a fourfold assembly including laypeople, and some use it for any practice group.
the Buddha said good friendship is the whole of the holy life
Ananda said half; the Buddha corrected him: the whole.
the sangha is one of the three jewels
the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.

games.q: you're Ananda. you tell the Buddha: good friendship seems to be half the holy life. how does he answer?
o: no, it's a distraction from practice.
no: it's the whole of the holy life.
games.why: the whole. a person with good friends, he says, can be expected to develop the entire path.

practice: The bell gives you about seventy-five seconds. Bring to mind the people who walk with you. Not the whole world, just a few faces.
The friend who checks in. The teacher who believed in you. Maybe the stranger who sat near you once, in a quiet room.
Hold each face for a breath or two. Notice that you didn't get here alone. If you like, let a little metta go to each of them.

wordCard.voice: The sangha. The community, the third jewel; the people who practice together and keep each other walking. Seventeenth word.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit: assembly, community. The third of the three jewels.

carryVoice: Your line: you need people. Not half the path, the Buddha said: the whole of it. Day seventeen.

sources.ref: Dhammapada 190 (Max Müller renders sangha as 'the Church')
